title: Upload & Transcoding
description: Design video upload with chunked resumable uploads, DAG-based transcoding pipelines, adaptive bitrate encoding ladders, thumbnail generation, and content fingerprinting.

segments.text: YouTube receives over five hundred hours of video every minute. A single four-K video can be several gigabytes. Upload over a mobile connection that drops frequently? You need chunked, resumable uploads. Google's resumable upload protocol splits files into chunks, tracks progress, and resumes from the last successful chunk.

Split the video into five-megabyte chunks. Upload each chunk with a Content-Range header. The server tracks which chunks are received using a bitmap. On connection failure, the client asks the server which chunks are missing and resumes. The tus protocol is the open standard for this — used by Vimeo, Cloudflare, and many others.

Once uploaded, the video enters a transcoding pipeline modeled as a DAG — directed acyclic graph. First: extract audio and video tracks. Then in parallel: transcode video to multiple resolutions, encode audio in multiple codecs, generate thumbnails, and run content fingerprinting. Dependencies define the execution order — thumbnails depend on video extraction but not on audio.

Adaptive bitrate encoding creates multiple quality versions. Netflix's per-title encoding analyzes each video's complexity and generates a custom bitrate ladder. A talking-head video looks great at 750 kilobits per second. An action scene needs 4500 kilobits. The encoding ladder might produce eight to twelve variants per video — from 240p to 4K.

Transcoding one hour of video takes roughly four hours of compute time. YouTube gets five hundred hours of video per minute. How many transcoding workers do you need, and how would you manage the queue?
segments.thought_prompt: Calculate the transcoding compute needed for 500 hours/minute of video uploads. How do you scale this?

segments.text: Thumbnail generation extracts key frames and optionally uses ML to select the most visually appealing frame. Netflix A/B tests different thumbnails per user — personalized thumbnails. They found that the right thumbnail increases click-through rate by twenty to thirty percent. Generate thumbnails at multiple sizes for different device contexts.

Content fingerprinting detects copyrighted material. YouTube's Content ID system generates a perceptual hash of each video — a fingerprint that survives transcoding, cropping, and speed changes. New uploads are compared against a database of over a hundred million reference files. Matches trigger automated claims — block, monetize, or track.

Storage for transcoded videos is massive. A single video in twelve quality variants with two audio tracks consumes roughly fifty times the original file size in storage. YouTube likely stores over a billion videos. Hot storage for popular content uses SSDs, warm storage for recent uploads uses HDDs, and cold storage for rarely accessed content uses tape or glacier.

Transcoding failures are common — codec bugs, out-of-memory errors, corrupt input. Each stage of the DAG must be independently retryable. If thumbnail generation fails, don't re-transcode the entire video. Track DAG state in a database and restart only the failed node. Use dead letter queues for videos that repeatedly fail and need manual investigation.
Design the upload and transcoding pipeline for a video platform handling ten thousand uploads per hour with a target of making videos playable within five minutes of upload completion.
segments.thought_prompt: Design an upload + transcoding pipeline for 10K uploads/hour with 5-minute processing target.

segments.text: Video upload and transcoding is a massive parallel processing problem. Chunked uploads handle unreliable connections, DAG-based pipelines maximize parallelism, adaptive bitrate ladders optimize quality per video, and content fingerprinting enables copyright protection. The scale of this system — hundreds of hours of video per minute — makes it one of the most compute-intensive systems to design.
